
## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

Task 1 review came back: **Spec ✅, quality Approved** — but with two findings to fix. Fix round 1 of 5.

**Finding 1 (Important) — `connect()` has zero test coverage, including its eagerness.**

All three of your tests exercise `connection_manager_config()` and `ConnectionManager::new_lazy_with_config`; none ever calls `connect()`. So the eager-`new_with_config` contract — which is a spec MUST, because it preserves `AppState::new`'s fail-fast-at-boot behavior — is guarded only by a human reading the source. A later edit swapping `new_with_config` for `new_lazy_with_config` inside `connect` would pass every existing test.

This is a gap in the brief I wrote, not a mistake you made. Fix it now.

The property is cheaply and *discriminatingly* testable without Docker: against a dead port, an **eager** `connect` returns `Err` (it awaits the initial connection), while a **lazy** one would return `Ok` (the manager builds fine; the error only surfaces on the first command). So the assertion actually distinguishes the two implementations rather than just exercising the happy path.

Add a fourth test to `adapters/redis_conn.rs`, in the same style as the existing three:

- `#[tokio::test]`, named for the property (e.g. `connect_is_eager_so_a_dead_backend_fails_at_construction`).
- Call `connect("redis://127.0.0.1:1").await` and assert it is `Err`.
- Assert `err.is_io_error()` as the control, same reasoning as the existing fast-fail test.
- Bound it with the same 2 s deadline — with the capped budget this must also be fast, and it is a second, independent witness that the config reaches the manager.
- The failure message must say explicitly that an `Ok` here means `connect` went lazy and `AppState::new` would no longer fail fast at boot (SMA-473 D10). Someone tripping this needs to know *why* laziness is wrong, not just that a test failed.

**Finding 2 (Minor) — make the dead-code attribute self-removing.**

Your `#[allow(dead_code, reason = "...")]` on `connect` is correctly justified and correctly scoped. Change `allow` to `expect`: `#[expect(dead_code, reason = "...")]`. Because the workspace denies `warnings` (which includes `unfulfilled_lint_expectations`), Task 2 wiring up the real callers will then turn the stale attribute into a hard compile error instead of leaving it to be silently forgotten. Keep the reason string.

Note this interacts with Finding 1: once your new test calls `connect()`, that may itself satisfy the dead-code check and make the `expect` unfulfilled *immediately*. If so, just drop the attribute entirely — that is the better outcome. Let the compiler tell you which it is; do not guess.

**Then:**
- Re-run `cargo nextest run -p paigasus-iam --lib adapters::redis_conn --no-tests=pass` and `cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and paste the real output.
- Append a fix-round section to your existing report file (`.../task-1-report.md`) with the covering tests, the exact commands, and their output.
- Commit (same commitlint rules: lowercase subject, ≤100 chars, no bare `#NNN`, no `--no-verify`).

Diff reviewed: `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/redis_conn.rs` (only file changed, 28 insertions / 1 deletion). Cross-checked against the live file and confirmed `Task 2` has not landed yet (`grep` for `redis_conn::connect` call sites in the crate found none — `entity_cache.rs`/`decision_cache.rs` still call `ConnectionManager::new(client)` directly), so the premise behind Finding 2's fix is still live.

### Finding 1 — `connect()` eagerness test: **ADDRESSED**

New test at `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/redis_conn.rs:167-184` (`connect_is_eager_so_a_dead_backend_fails_at_construction`):
- Calls `connect("redis://127.0.0.1:1").await` directly (line 170) — not a hand-built manager.
- `result.expect_err(...)` (line 173) with a message stating an `Ok` means `connect` went lazy and `AppState::new` would no longer fail fast at boot (SMA-473 D10) — matches the required wording.
- `err.is_io_error()` control (line 177), same pattern as the pre-existing `a_command_against_an_unreachable_backend_fails_fast` test.
- `elapsed < Duration::from_secs(2)` deadline (lines 179-183).

**Discrimination check verified, not just asserted.** `connect` (line 61-64) awaits `ConnectionManager::new_with_config(...)`, which dials during construction. Against `127.0.0.1:1` (closed port, immediate `ECONNREFUSED`) this resolves to `Err` fast. If `connect` were swapped to `new_lazy_with_config` (per the doc comment at lines 159-166 and confirmed by the crate's own existing test-3 comment "`lazy ConnectionManager construction never connects`" at line 131), construction would succeed and return `Ok` — the connection error would only surface on the first command, which this test never issues. So the test genuinely fails under a lazy swap rather than passing either way. The doc comment on lines 159-166 correctly states this reasoning.

### Finding 2 — `cfg_attr(not(test), expect(...))` resolution: **ADDRESSED, reasoning holds**

Current code, `redis_conn.rs:60`:
```rust
#[cfg_attr(not(test), expect(dead_code, reason = "Task 2 (SMA-473) wires up the 8 call sites; unused until then"))]
```

Verified independently (not just trusting the report's build logs):
- `rs/Cargo.toml:161` sets `[workspace.lints.rust] warnings = "deny"`; `paigasus-iam/Cargo.toml:144-145` has `[lints] workspace = true` — so both `dead_code` and `unfulfilled_lint_expectations` (a default-warn lint, part of the `warnings` group) are hard-denied crate-wide, confirming the report's compiler-error evidence is architecturally consistent, not a fluke.
- The split is real and necessary: in the `cfg(test)` unittest binary, `connect` is now called by the new Finding-1 test, so a bare `expect(dead_code)` there would be *unfulfilled* (nothing to suppress) → hard error. In the plain `--lib` build (no `cfg(test)`), Task 2 hasn't landed, so `connect` is genuinely unreached → a bare *absence* of the attribute would hard-error there instead. `cfg_attr(not(test), expect(...))` puts the attribute only in the compilation mode where the dead-code condition can actually be true, which is exactly the mode split clippy's `--all-targets` exercises (plain lib target vs. `cfg(test)` unit-test target).
- **Self-removing property confirmed preserved**: once Task 2 adds a real, non-test caller, the plain-mode (`not(test)` = true) `expect(dead_code)` will no longer see the lint fire (function is used) → `unfulfilled_lint_expectations` fires → denied by `warnings = "deny"` → hard compile error forcing removal. This is the same mechanism, just correctly scoped to the one mode where it stays meaningful over time.
- **Narrowest tool check**: given Rust has no per-compilation-mode conditional lint syntax other than `cfg_attr`, and the dead-code truth value genuinely differs between the two modes (not a policy choice, a real fact about reachability), `cfg_attr` isn't a workaround bolted on for convenience — it's the direct encoding of "this attribute is only meaningful/needed in mode X." A bare `allow` in the `cfg_attr` (instead of `expect`) would compile fine in both modes but silently reintroduce the exact staleness problem Finding 2 was raised to close, so `expect` inside the conditional is required, not just `allow`. No simpler construct (e.g., a manual "phantom use" shim) would be simpler or safer — it would just reimplement the same idea more awkwardly. Confirmed as the narrowest correct tool.
- Reachability propagation (`connection_manager_config`, `CONNECT_RETRIES`, `RETRY_MAX_DELAY` staying clean because `connect` is treated as a live root once the lint is suppressed) is unchanged from the original `allow`-based mechanism from the prior round — `expect` and `allow` share that suppression semantics, only differing in whether the "did it fire" check is applied.

No new imports, no test-name collisions, no lint-suppression gaps beyond the one intentionally scoped by `cfg_attr`. Line lengths (e.g. `redis_conn.rs:140`) are within the workspace's `rustfmt.toml` `max_width = 200` (confirmed by reading `rs/rustfmt.toml`), consistent with the file's pre-existing style — not a regression.

- `redis_conn.rs:60` — the `cfg_attr(not(test), ...)` line has no inline comment explaining *why* it's mode-conditional; that rationale currently lives only in `task-1-report.md`. A future reader hitting this line cold (without the report) may find the construction non-obvious. Worth a short comment if this module gets touched again before Task 2 lands, but not a defect.

```yaml
      offenders="$(printf '%s\n' "$hits" | grep -v '^\./adapters/redis_conn\.rs:' || true)"

    toolchain: 'system'

    inputs:
      - 'rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/**/*'
```

```yaml
  redis-connect-single-site:
    description: 'Assert redis connection config is owned solely by `adapters::redis_conn`, so no call site can restore the unbounded reconnect retry budget (SMA-473).'
    # WHAT IS GATED, and why it is not simply "ConnectionManager::new":
    #   - `ConnectionManager::new(` / `::new_with_config(` — the eager constructors the
    #     helper owns. Allowed only in redis_conn.rs.
    #   - the `ConnectionManagerConfig` TYPE — naming it is how you would build an untuned
    #     config. Allowed only in redis_conn.rs.
    # `ConnectionManager::new_lazy_with_config(...)` is deliberately NOT gated: two
    # `#[cfg(test)]` sites legitimately call it, and they are safe precisely because the
    # rule above means the only config they can obtain is `connection_manager_config()`.
    #
    # Comment lines are excluded so prose may still name the API.
    #
    # Two portability notes, both learned the hard way:
    #   - Do NOT anchor paths on `^\./`. GNU grep (CI, Linux) emits the `./` prefix; ugrep
    #     (some dev shells) strips it. An `^\./` anchor silently matches nothing on one of
    #     them, which would make this gate pass while guarding nothing.
    #   - The comment filter anchors on `:[0-9]+:[[:space:]]*//` so it tests the CONTENT,
    #     not any `://` that happens to appear inside a redis URL on a code line.
    #
    # The control (`expected` must be non-empty) matters: without it, a rename of
    # redis_conn.rs — or a typo in the pattern — would make BOTH greps empty and the gate
    # would pass while guarding nothing.
    script: |
      cd rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src
      hits="$(grep -rnE 'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig' . | grep -vE ':[0-9]+:[[:space:]]*//' || true)"
      expected="$(printf '%s\n' "$hits" | grep -E 'adapters/redis_conn\.rs:' || true)"
      offenders="$(printf '%s\n' "$hits" | grep -vE 'adapters/redis_conn\.rs:' || true)"
      if [ -z "$expected" ]; then
        echo "no redis connection-config construction found in adapters/redis_conn.rs — the guard is not guarding anything (renamed file? changed API?)" >&2
        exit 2
      fi
      if [ -n "$offenders" ]; then
        echo "redis connection config built outside adapters/redis_conn.rs (SMA-473 — use redis_conn::connect / connection_manager_config):" >&2
        printf '%s\n' "$offenders" >&2
        exit 1
      fi
    toolchain: 'system'
    # Narrow inputs — `repo` owns the whole tree, so without these the guard runs on every change.
    inputs:
      - 'rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/**/*'
```

**Note on the probe in Step 3 below:** it must name something the gate actually
catches. `ConnectionManager::new` without a paren is *not* gated (that is the bare
path, and `new_lazy_with_config` must stay legal outside the helper) — use
`ConnectionManagerConfig::new()` in the probe instead.

Task 4 review: **Spec ✅, quality Approved**, but with two Important findings. Fix round 1 of 5. The reviewer built rule mutants and ran promtool against them, so these are empirical, not speculative.

**Finding 1 (Important) — the fixture's control comment explains the wrong thing.**

Your comment (from my brief, so this is my error not yours) claims the `cache="hit"` series plus the `eval_time: 5m` assertion is what catches a rule that dropped its `cache="bypass"` selector or used `>= 0`. That is false. The reviewer proved it:

- `eval_time: 5m` run in isolation against **both** mutants → SUCCESS. It does not fail.
- `5m` + `20m` only, omitting `12m`, against the selector-dropped mutant → SUCCESS. Still passes.
- The full fixture does fail on both mutants — but promtool reports the failure at `time: 12m` in both cases.

The reason: `for: 10m` guarantees nothing can be *active* at 5m no matter what the expression says. The real discriminator is **`eval_time: 12m`**: under the correct rule the genuine bypass signal has only been true ~6 minutes by then and is still pending, whereas under either mutant the `hit` series (or `>= 0` against the flat-zero segment) has been true since ~t=1m, so `for: 10m` has already elapsed and it fires early.

Rewrite the fixture's leading comment to say this accurately. The point of that comment is to encode the SMA-466 lesson about self-deceiving test rationale — a comment that misidentifies its own discriminator is exactly the failure it is meant to prevent. Specifically:
- Name `eval_time: 12m` as the assertion that does the discriminating work, and say why (correct rule = still pending at 12m; either mutant = `for` already elapsed and firing).
- Keep the `eval_time: 5m` case, but describe it honestly as what it is — a sanity check that a healthy window is quiet — not as the mutation catcher.
- Keep the `cache="hit"` control series; it is still what makes the 12m assertion discriminate.

**Finding 2 (Important) — the memory-backend silent trap needs to be an annotation, not just a `#` comment.**

Your rule has `annotations: { summary: ... }` only. The prose about `authz.cache.backend = "memory"` making the alert silent lives in a `#` comment, which is invisible on Prometheus's `/rules` page and in Alertmanager — only someone reading the committed YAML sees it.

- **Gateway M5** observability: provider-routing, cost/budget, and response-cache metrics, and a
  corresponding dashboard extension — those surfaces (multi-provider routing, caching, budgets)
  don't exist yet; this cycle scoped gateway metrics to the M0 auth+proxy surface only.
- **A combined IAM introspect-and-authorize RPC**, which would also reduce the gateway's
  per-request round-trip count and the surface area of `GatewayIamDependencyUnavailable`.
- **A capped Redis reconnect-retry schedule** (`ConnectionManagerConfig::set_number_of_retries` /
  `set_max_delay` on `connect_redis`'s `ConnectionManager`, plus a circuit breaker that stops
  attempting Redis once the backend is known-down). This is the named mitigation for the
  ~20–30 s per-decision cost that §4 "Authz availability posture" documents. Note the knob is the
  retry schedule, **not** `connection_timeout`/`response_timeout` — those are already bounded by
  redis-rs's defaults (1 s / 500 ms). Until it lands, a Redis outage degrades authz availability
  far more than the word "fail-open" implies. Tracked as **SMA-473**; pre-existing, not

Summary: rewrote the RUNBOOK's authz-availability cost/detection/revocation prose to the shipped ~0.2–0.8 s bound, added the `IamAuthzRedisCacheBypassed` catalog entry + table row, reduced the §6 limitation bullet to the circuit breaker, and updated the `cedar_authorizer.rs` module doc and the acceptance-test comments.

Concerns worth your eye:
1. I dropped `maxmemory` eviction from the alert's **Likely causes** — an evicted counter is a *missing* key, which `Generations::read` maps to `0` (a successful read), so it silently rewinds rather than emitting `cache="bypass"`. Kept memory pressure only in its erroring forms, with an explicit "not in this list" note.
2. The three caches have independent `redis_url`s, so I qualified the blast radius with "if the *same* Redis also backs …" rather than asserting one outage hits all three.
3. The acceptance test sets `policy_cache_ttl_secs = 1` / `refresh_interval_secs = 1`, so its `ttl + poll` is ~2 s, not the ~31 s defaults — the comment says ~2 s.
4. Soft numbers I rounded: "~10×" for the blackhole multiplier (really 10–20×) and "~50× sooner" for boot tolerance (really 30–60×); "~2.1 s" for a blackholed backend is analytic in `redis_conn.rs`, never measured.

/// install budget below is deliberately an order of magnitude wider than `ttl + poll`, because

Outside the brief's `~705-720` window, but same test, same file, same commit — a reader now gets two incompatible justifications for the same 90 s budget.

**4. Analytic vs. measured is inferable, not stated — for the one number operators are told to multiply.** `:757` gives `~2.1 s` with its derivation shown ("two 1 s attempts plus the ~100–200 ms delay"), then `:758` says "Multiply the 'cycles' column by that". **5. "~50× sooner" (`:763`) vs. 30–60×.** `redis_conn.rs:54-55` gives ~6–12 s → ~200 ms. 50× is the top of the range, not the middle. Low harm — the very next sentence gives both raw windows, so the claim self-corrects. `~30–60×` would be strictly right.

**6. "~10× the table" (`:753`) vs. 10–21×.** Conservative floor, and the actionable instruction (`× 2.1 s`) is exact, so the heading multiplier is decorative. Not misleading.

**7. `:786-787` "every authenticated request `503`s" vs. `:797` "requests keep succeeding".** Read literally, adjacent paragraphs contradict. "Every *token*-authenticated request" would remove it. Brief-prescribed wording.

**8. Blast-radius qualifier applied inconsistently.** `:575-576` correctly notes each cache has its own `redis_url`; the parallel list at `:777-779` ("per-replica API-key revocation") does not carry the caveat.

Findings 1–3 are mechanical edits. With those applied I'd approve.

**Finding 3 (Important) — stale test doc comment: ADDRESSED.** `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/tests/authz_acceptance.rs:615-623` now says the budget is wide *not* because the outage stretches cadence, and inverts the RUNBOOK cross-reference to what that section now says (`RUNBOOK-observability.md:828`, "That bound now holds during a Redis outage too"). It is consistent with the inline comment at `authz_acceptance.rs:710-724`. The 90 s budget is unchanged.

Verified in source: `adapters/http/auth_middleware.rs:51` routes an `api_key_prefix` credential to `api_key_auth.resolve`, which never touches the JWKS path, and `adapters/api_keys/cache.rs:279-295` fails open onto Postgres. **(c) independent-`redis_url` caveat: ADDRESSED** (`:789-793`), matching the qualifier at `:584-585`.

**Deferred items untouched: confirmed.** "~50× sooner" (`:775`) and "~10× the table" (`:763`) are context-only in the diff.

**Previously-verified claims: no regression.** The `max_delay`-unset sentence (`:728-730`) is context-only in the diff and unedited. The three revocation claims survive verbatim at `:837-841`. `cedar_authorizer.rs` is not in the fix diff at all; "an accelerator outage costs latency, never correctness" is intact at `cedar_authorizer.rs:35-36`.

The extended "not a cause" note is accurate.** Verified against source, not the report: `Generations::read` is `conn.get(key)` (`adapters/authz/generation.rs:86`) with `val.unwrap_or(0)` on a missing key (`:87`); `Generations::bump` is `conn.incr(key, 1_i64)` (`:100`). `GET` is `readonly fast` / not `denyoom`; `INCR` is `write denyoom fast`. I have everything I need. Here is the review.

---

# Whole-branch review — `feature/sma-473-iam-bound-redis-retry-budget`

**Independently verified before writing this:** `cargo fmt --check` clean; `cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -D warnings` clean; `promtool check rules` + `test rules` green; `repo:redis-connect-single-site` green; `observability-drift` green; the headline test numbers reproduce (`redis_cache_fails_open_when_the_backend_is_unreachable` **0.469 s**, `redis_conn` probes 0.162 s ≈ one 100–200 ms cycle). The mechanism claims check out against the vendored `redis-1.3.0` source, and the 2/3-cycle counts check out against `PolicySnapshot::reload_if_stale`'s early return on `!trusted`. Commit subjects are lowercase, ≤100 chars, scoped, no bare `#NNN`. SPDX header present on the one new source file. CODEOWNERS untouched.

No Critical findings.

## Important

### I1. The CI gate does not catch `redis::Client::get_connection_manager()` — redis-rs's own one-liner for the stock 6-retry config
`moon.yml:170`

The gate matches three strings: `ConnectionManager::new(`, `ConnectionManager::new_with_config(`, `ConnectionManagerConfig`. But `redis-1.3.0/src/client.rs:453` provides:

```rust
pub async fn get_connection_manager(&self) -> RedisResult<crate::aio::ConnectionManager> {
    crate::aio::ConnectionManager::new(self.clone()).await   // <- stock ConnectionManagerConfig::new()
}
```

I proved the miss:

```
$ printf 'let conn = redis::Client::open(url)?.get_connection_manager().await?;\n' \
    | grep -nE 'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig'
GATE MISSES (exit 1)
```

Also missed: `client.get_connection_manager_with_config(Default::default())` and `client.get_connection_manager_lazy(Default::default())`.

This is not the deliberate-alias evasion the ledger deferred. `client.get_connection_manager()` is the **first** `ConnectionManager` example in redis-rs's own docs and the most natural thing a future contributor reaches for — it is precisely the accidental/copy-paste bypass the gate exists to stop. Spec §4.3 (`…design.md:361-362`) calls this gate "the only thing that catches a *new* call site added later"; as shipped, it isn't.

**Failure scenario:** SMA-4xx adds a Redis-backed rate-limit or session cache in `paigasus-iam` and wires it `let conn = redis::Client::open(url)?.get_connection_manager().await?;`. `repo:redis-connect-single-site` is green. §4.1's config test is green (it asserts on `connection_manager_config()`, which is still correct — it's simply not used). That connection silently carries the stock 6-retry budget: ~9.5 s per failed command, and if it sits on a request path, 19–28 s per request during a Redis outage — the exact regression this branch exists to prevent, reintroduced under a green CI.

**Fix (one alternation term, no false positives — zero uses in the tree today):**
```
'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig|\.get_connection_manager'
```
This also correctly forces the `_with_config` / `_lazy` variants through `redis_conn.rs`, which is where they belong anyway.

I consider this must-fix-before-merge: it is the AC4 deliverable itself, and it is a one-token change.

### I2. The change also makes the fail-closed JWKS path fail *more often*, not just faster — and D6 asserts the opposite
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-sma-473-redis-retry-budget-design.md:171-173` (D6), `:434-438` (residual), `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:796-805`

D6 says: *"This changes **only how fast** the JWKS path fails; the D15 fail-closed posture is untouched and stays correct."* That is false in a way the branch's own residual list half-notices and then mis-scopes.

Mechanism (verified in `connection_manager.rs:570-591`): when the shared connection future is being re-established, the *first* command awaits the full `backon` schedule. Pre-fix that schedule ran for up to ~9.5 s, so a Redis blip/failover **shorter than the schedule was absorbed and the command succeeded** (just slowly). Post-fix the absorption window is a single 100–200 ms retry.

- On the authz path this is a cache bypass — fail-open, harmless, and the spec's residual records it (`:434-438`: *"correctness is unaffected… briefly noisier `cache="bypass"`"*).
- On `authn.jwks_cache.backend = "redis"` the identical event is a `503` on **every token-authenticated request**, because `RedisJwksCache::get`'s error is `?`-propagated out of `JwksProvider::cache_state` (`jwks.rs:249`) before any refetch is attempted. The residual is written only for the fail-open half; nothing anywhere covers the fail-closed half.

**Failure scenario:** a routine Redis primary failover lasting 2 s. Before this branch: authentication unaffected — the JWKS `get` waits out the gap and succeeds. After: every OIDC-bearer request `503`s for those 2 s. `IamHighErrorRate`/`IamGrpcHighErrorRate` don't fire (2 s ≪ `for: 10m`). `IamAuthzRedisCacheBypassed` doesn't fire either (same `for: 10m`, deliberately). The operator sees a 2-second authentication outage with **no alert and no document predicting it** — which is the "trades a loud failure for a silent one" shape this branch was specifically designed to avoid.

The fix is documentation (correct D6, widen the residual, add a sentence to the RUNBOOK's JWKS paragraph at `:796`). But the team should take the underlying decision consciously: a fail-closed path arguably wants a larger connect budget than a fail-open one, and D8's single shared `connection_manager_config()` currently forbids that. Recording it as a deliberate accepted trade is enough; silently asserting it doesn't exist is not.

## Minor

### M3. "ten straight minutes" is wrong — the alert can page after ~5 minutes of bypassing
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:541-545`

`rate(...[5m])` stays `> 0` for a full 5 m after the *last* bypass sample. So `for: 10m` is satisfied by a bypass window of only ~5 minutes. The "Meaning" paragraph's *"bypassed entirely for ten straight minutes"* and the reasoning *"Ten minutes of it means the Redis backend is unhealthy"* both overstate by 2×; the real failover tolerance is ~5 minutes, not 10. The `for: 10m` choice is still right — only the explanation is wrong, and it's the first thing a paged operator reads.

### M4. The one un-reconciled number, plus a historical claim that is provably false
`ops/observability/prometheus/rules/iam.rules.yml:79`

> `# announced itself as ~20-30s authz latency that tripped IamHighErrorRate and client timeouts`

(a) Every other file settled on **19–28 s**; `~20-30s` is the pre-revision figure. This is the only remaining inconsistent number I found across the spec, `redis_conn.rs`, `cedar_authorizer.rs`, the RUNBOOK, the alert annotations and the test comments.

(b) `IamHighErrorRate` **could not have fired** from authz latency. `serve_http` (`adapters/http/mod.rs:733-735`) applies `TimeoutLayer` *outside* `app_routes`, which carries `http_metrics_layer` inside it — so a timed-out request short-circuits at 408 before the metrics layer records anything, and `iam_http_requests_total` never counts it at all. Even if it did, 408 is `status_class="4xx"` (`paigasus-observability/src/http.rs:71`) and the rule filters `5xx`. The gRPC half (`IamGrpcHighErrorRate`, `grpc_status != "ok"`) does hold. The same historical framing appears at RUNBOOK `:783-786`, where it's forward-looking and therefore harmless.

This *strengthens* the case for the new alert — the old HTTP signal was weaker than the branch credits it with — but the claim should be corrected rather than shipped as fact.

### M5. Two different per-decision bounds
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:548`, `:707`, `:1125` say **~0.2–0.8 s per authz decision**; `cedar_authorizer.rs:45` says **~0.2-0.6 s per decision**. Both are right at their own scope, but the 0.8 s upper end comes from the *revoke* row (a mutation), not any decision row in the table. Suggested single formulation: *0.2–0.6 s per decision; 0.3–0.8 s per authz-mutating request; up to ~1.2 s for a gated cross-principal decision.*

### M6. The gate is scoped to `src/` only; AC1 says "production and test"
`moon.yml:169` and `:186`. I confirmed `tests/` currently contains only prose mentions of `ConnectionManager` (`authz_acceptance.rs:449,710`, `authz_generations_redis.rs:5`), so nothing is wrong today — but a new Docker-gated integration test can construct a stock manager without CI noticing. Adding `tests/` to the `cd` scope and to `inputs` closes it.

### M7. Spec §4.3 / AC4 no longer describe the shipped gate
`…design.md:358-359` and `:468` still say the gate asserts `new_lazy_with_config` appears only in `redis_conn.rs`. The Task 3 plan-defect correction (correctly) exempted it — two `#[cfg(test)]` sites legitimately call it. The spec was never updated. This is exactly the "Task N's assumption invalidated by Task M" class; it matters because the spec is the artifact a future reader will consult before touching the gate.

### M8. Stale mechanism attribution
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:725-726`: *"both applied to every attempt by `new_lazy_with_config`"*. Production now uses `new_with_config`, and both constructors apply the timeouts identically. Carry-over from the pre-fix text; reads as if the timeouts only apply on the lazy path.

### M9. The alert's remediation omits the one new capacity risk the fix creates
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:577-596`. "Blast radius" correctly says *"every decision pays a raw Postgres entity-slice load"* — but the fix also removes the accidental ~50× throttle that the retry latency imposed, so the **uncached** decision rate hitting Postgres during an outage is now full traffic rather than trickle. It is not silent (sqlx pool saturation → 5xx → `IamHighErrorRate`), so this isn't a correctness problem — but "check Postgres/pool headroom" belongs in **Confirm**, since it's the failure mode the change newly enables.

### M10. Naming collision in prose
`adapters/http/mod.rs:626-628`: *"when it can't reuse an already-open `redis_conn`"* refers to the local `redis_conn: Option<ConnectionManager>` binding at `:291`. There is now also a module `crate::adapters::redis_conn`. One word of disambiguation.

### M11. (Informational — closes an open spec question)
Spec `:428-430` records: *"**Unverified:** whether `connection_timeout` also wraps DNS resolution."* It does. `redis-1.3.0/src/client.rs:505-510` wraps the entire `get_multiplexed_async_connection_inner` — address resolution included — in `rt.timeout(connection_timeout, …)`. So the ~2.1 s blackhole figure holds for a hung DNS resolver too, and that residual can be stated as verified rather than open.

## Answers to the four framing questions

**1. Cross-task coherence.** The six tasks compose correctly. Numbers are consistent everywhere I checked (cycle counts ↔ 9.5 s/cycle before, 0.1–0.2 s/cycle after; 28.403/3 = 9.47; 0.471/3 = 0.157). The only genuine drift is **M4(a)** (`~20-30s` in the rule comment) and the scope mismatch in **M5**. The one place a later task invalidated an earlier artifact without updating it is **M7**.

**2. Did it achieve the actual goal?** Yes, on the measured shape. I looked for anything still unbounded on the operator's end-to-end path and found nothing: per-attempt timeouts are bounded (1 s / 500 ms, DNS included per M11), the retry schedule is now one 100–200 ms step, `reload_if_stale` short-circuits once the stamp goes provisional, and HTTP/gRPC both carry a 30 s request timeout (`main.rs:66`). The *cost* of the win is that the bottleneck moves to Postgres (M9) and that fail-closed blips stop being absorbed (I2). Neither is unbounded; both should be written down.

**3. The declines.** D1 (leave the timeouts), D7 (no breaker), D4 (no config surface) are all still defensible as shipped — D1 in particular is now better supported, since M11 shows `connection_timeout` genuinely bounds the blackhole shape end-to-end. **D10's boot tolerance is safe** as reasoned: `AppState::new` fails fast (`http/mod.rs:301`), `main.rs:60` has no retry loop, and the process exits — verified. The one soft spot is that D10's justification leans on "container restart backoff (10 s → 20 s → 40 s)", which is Kubernetes `CrashLoopBackOff` specifically; the repo ships no deployment manifest for IAM, so nothing guarantees it. Under a supervisor with a fixed short restart delay, IAM now crash-loops ~30–50× faster than before during a Redis outage. Not a blocker (no manifest exists to be wrong), but the RUNBOOK's *"Depend on the orchestrator's restart policy"* at `:780-781` is doing real load-bearing work and should say "verify your orchestrator actually has backoff". **The JWKS fail-closed posture was correctly not reopened** — but see I2: the branch changed its *failure frequency* without saying so.

**4. The alert, end-to-end.** Verified line by line and it holds up:
- `cache="bypass"` is emitted at exactly one site, `cedar_authorizer.rs:251-252`, reachable only when `cache_key()` returned `None`, i.e. `gens.entity_gen()` errored — matches the RUNBOOK's claim verbatim.
- PromQL is byte-identical across `iam.rules.yml:73`, the catalog table (`RUNBOOK:199`), the entry body (`:541`) and the detection paragraph (`:787`).
- Severity `critical` / `for: 10m` consistent in all four places; annotations byte-identical between rule and fixture (promtool enforces that).
- Confirm step 3's log strings both exist verbatim: `cedar_authorizer.rs:167` and `redis_cache.rs:72`.
- Confirm step 4's `authz.cache.redis_url`, and the remediation's `authz.cache.backend`, `api_keys.introspect_cache.ttl_secs`, `authn.jwks_cache.backend` are all real config keys (`config.rs:51,97,205`).
- `up{job="iam"}` matches `prometheus.yml`'s `job_name: iam`.
- The `memory`-backend silence trap is real and correctly explained.
- The fixture's control series is genuinely load-bearing (the ledger's empirical mutant check matches my reading of the `for: 10m` × `eval_time: 12m` interaction).

Two caveats: **M3** (the "ten minutes" arithmetic) and the fact that under `authz.cache.backend = "memory"` + `api_keys.introspect_cache.backend = "redis"` there is now **no** Redis signal at all. I checked that second one and it's benign — `authz.cache = memory` is single-replica-only by construction, and on a single replica the degraded behaviour (per-replica TTL, fail-open onto Postgres) is what the memory backend does anyway. Not worth a finding.

## Deferred-minors triage

| # | Item | Verdict |

# Whole-branch review — `feature/sma-473-iam-bound-redis-retry-budget`

**Independently verified before writing this:** `cargo fmt --check` clean; `cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -D warnings` clean; `promtool check rules` + `test rules` green; `repo:redis-connect-single-site` green; `observability-drift` green; the headline test numbers reproduce (`redis_cache_fails_open_when_the_backend_is_unreachable` **0.469 s**, `redis_conn` probes 0.162 s ≈ one 100–200 ms cycle). The mechanism claims check out against the vendored `redis-1.3.0` source, and the 2/3-cycle counts check out against `PolicySnapshot::reload_if_stale`'s early return on `!trusted`. Commit subjects are lowercase, ≤100 chars, scoped, no bare `#NNN`. SPDX header present on the one new source file. CODEOWNERS untouched.

No Critical findings.

## Important

### I1. The CI gate does not catch `redis::Client::get_connection_manager()` — redis-rs's own one-liner for the stock 6-retry config
`moon.yml:170`

The gate matches three strings: `ConnectionManager::new(`, `ConnectionManager::new_with_config(`, `ConnectionManagerConfig`. But `redis-1.3.0/src/client.rs:453` provides:

```rust
pub async fn get_connection_manager(&self) -> RedisResult<crate::aio::ConnectionManager> {
    crate::aio::ConnectionManager::new(self.clone()).await   // <- stock ConnectionManagerConfig::new()
}
```

I proved the miss:

```
$ printf 'let conn = redis::Client::open(url)?.get_connection_manager().await?;\n' \
    | grep -nE 'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig'
GATE MISSES (exit 1)
```

Also missed: `client.get_connection_manager_with_config(Default::default())` and `client.get_connection_manager_lazy(Default::default())`.

This is not the deliberate-alias evasion the ledger deferred. `client.get_connection_manager()` is the **first** `ConnectionManager` example in redis-rs's own docs and the most natural thing a future contributor reaches for — it is precisely the accidental/copy-paste bypass the gate exists to stop. Spec §4.3 (`…design.md:361-362`) calls this gate "the only thing that catches a *new* call site added later"; as shipped, it isn't.

**Failure scenario:** SMA-4xx adds a Redis-backed rate-limit or session cache in `paigasus-iam` and wires it `let conn = redis::Client::open(url)?.get_connection_manager().await?;`. `repo:redis-connect-single-site` is green. §4.1's config test is green (it asserts on `connection_manager_config()`, which is still correct — it's simply not used). That connection silently carries the stock 6-retry budget: ~9.5 s per failed command, and if it sits on a request path, 19–28 s per request during a Redis outage — the exact regression this branch exists to prevent, reintroduced under a green CI.

**Fix (one alternation term, no false positives — zero uses in the tree today):**
```
'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig|\.get_connection_manager'
```
This also correctly forces the `_with_config` / `_lazy` variants through `redis_conn.rs`, which is where they belong anyway.

I consider this must-fix-before-merge: it is the AC4 deliverable itself, and it is a one-token change.

### I2. The change also makes the fail-closed JWKS path fail *more often*, not just faster — and D6 asserts the opposite
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-sma-473-redis-retry-budget-design.md:171-173` (D6), `:434-438` (residual), `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:796-805`

D6 says: *"This changes **only how fast** the JWKS path fails; the D15 fail-closed posture is untouched and stays correct."* That is false in a way the branch's own residual list half-notices and then mis-scopes.

Mechanism (verified in `connection_manager.rs:570-591`): when the shared connection future is being re-established, the *first* command awaits the full `backon` schedule. Pre-fix that schedule ran for up to ~9.5 s, so a Redis blip/failover **shorter than the schedule was absorbed and the command succeeded** (just slowly). Post-fix the absorption window is a single 100–200 ms retry.

- On the authz path this is a cache bypass — fail-open, harmless, and the spec's residual records it (`:434-438`: *"correctness is unaffected… briefly noisier `cache="bypass"`"*).
- On `authn.jwks_cache.backend = "redis"` the identical event is a `503` on **every token-authenticated request**, because `RedisJwksCache::get`'s error is `?`-propagated out of `JwksProvider::cache_state` (`jwks.rs:249`) before any refetch is attempted. The residual is written only for the fail-open half; nothing anywhere covers the fail-closed half.

**Failure scenario:** a routine Redis primary failover lasting 2 s. Before this branch: authentication unaffected — the JWKS `get` waits out the gap and succeeds. After: every OIDC-bearer request `503`s for those 2 s. `IamHighErrorRate`/`IamGrpcHighErrorRate` don't fire (2 s ≪ `for: 10m`). `IamAuthzRedisCacheBypassed` doesn't fire either (same `for: 10m`, deliberately). The operator sees a 2-second authentication outage with **no alert and no document predicting it** — which is the "trades a loud failure for a silent one" shape this branch was specifically designed to avoid.

The fix is documentation (correct D6, widen the residual, add a sentence to the RUNBOOK's JWKS paragraph at `:796`). But the team should take the underlying decision consciously: a fail-closed path arguably wants a larger connect budget than a fail-open one, and D8's single shared `connection_manager_config()` currently forbids that. Recording it as a deliberate accepted trade is enough; silently asserting it doesn't exist is not.

## Minor

### M3. "ten straight minutes" is wrong — the alert can page after ~5 minutes of bypassing
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:541-545`

`rate(...[5m])` stays `> 0` for a full 5 m after the *last* bypass sample. So `for: 10m` is satisfied by a bypass window of only ~5 minutes. The "Meaning" paragraph's *"bypassed entirely for ten straight minutes"* and the reasoning *"Ten minutes of it means the Redis backend is unhealthy"* both overstate by 2×; the real failover tolerance is ~5 minutes, not 10. The `for: 10m` choice is still right — only the explanation is wrong, and it's the first thing a paged operator reads.

`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:548`, `:707`, `:1125` say **~0.2–0.8 s per authz decision**; `cedar_authorizer.rs:45` says **~0.2-0.6 s per decision**. `moon.yml:169` and `:186`. Adding `tests/` to the `cd` scope and to `inputs` closes it.

The Task 3 plan-defect correction (correctly) exempted it — two `#[cfg(test)]` sites legitimately call it. The spec was never updated. This is exactly the "Task N's assumption invalidated by Task M" class; it matters because the spec is the artifact a future reader will consult before touching the gate.

`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:725-726`: *"both applied to every attempt by `new_lazy_with_config`"*. Production now uses `new_with_config`, and both constructors apply the timeouts identically. Carry-over from the pre-fix text; reads as if the timeouts only apply on the lazy path.

### M9. The alert's remediation omits the one new capacity risk the fix creates
`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:577-596`. "Blast radius" correctly says *"every decision pays a raw Postgres entity-slice load"* — but the fix also removes the accidental ~50× throttle that the retry latency imposed, so the **uncached** decision rate hitting Postgres during an outage is now full traffic rather than trickle. **Context.** SMA-473 capped `paigasus-iam`'s Redis reconnect retry budget (6 retries → 1) behind a new `adapters::redis_conn` module that every construction site routes through, plus a CI gate enforcing that, a Prometheus alert for the outage the fix makes quiet, and operator docs. Measured: a unit test went 28.403 s → 0.471 s; the SMA-470 acceptance test 58 s → 3.227 s. The full graph passes. Six tasks each passed their own review; this is the last gate.

**Global constraints:**
- Prefix every shell command with `export PATH="$HOME/.proto/shims:$HOME/.proto/bin:$PATH"`.
- Conventional commit, workspace scope, **subject lowercase, ≤100 chars**, no bare `#NNN` in the body — write `SMA-473`.
- Do NOT use `git commit --no-verify`. If a commit fails with `1Password: failed to fill whole buffer`, STOP and report it as a blocker.
- `warnings = "deny"`; run `cargo clippy -p paigasus-iam --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` before committing.
- `.github/CODEOWNERS` is Moon-generated — never hand-edit.

## REQUIRED — I1: the CI gate has a hole at redis-rs's own first-choice API

`moon.yml:170`. The gate matches `ConnectionManager::new(`, `ConnectionManager::new_with_config(`, `ConnectionManagerConfig`. It misses `redis::Client::get_connection_manager()`, which at `redis-1.3.0/src/client.rs:453` is:

```rust
pub async fn get_connection_manager(&self) -> RedisResult<crate::aio::ConnectionManager> {
    crate::aio::ConnectionManager::new(self.clone()).await   // stock 6-retry config
}
```

Also missed: `get_connection_manager_with_config(...)` and `get_connection_manager_lazy(...)`. This is not a deliberate-alias evasion (which we deliberately do not chase) — it is the **first** `ConnectionManager` example in redis-rs's own docs, i.e. exactly the accidental/copy-paste bypass the gate exists to stop.

**Fix:** add `\.get_connection_manager` as a fourth alternation term:
```
'ConnectionManager::new\(|ConnectionManager::new_with_config\(|ConnectionManagerConfig|\.get_connection_manager'
```
Verified zero occurrences in the tree today, so no false positives. Update the gate's explanatory comment to say why this term is there (it catches the `Client` convenience constructors, which internally use the stock config).

**Also (M6):** the gate is scoped to `src/` only, but AC1 says "production and test". `tests/` currently has only prose mentions, but a new Docker-gated integration test could construct a stock manager unnoticed. Widen the `cd` scope and the `inputs:` glob to cover the crate's `tests/` directory as well. Make sure the existing prose mentions in `tests/authz_acceptance.rs` and `tests/authz_generations_redis.rs` do not trip it — they are `//`-comment lines, which the filter already excludes; **verify this by running the gate, do not assume**.

**Prove it, as Task 3 did:** run the gate (expect PASS), append a probe using `.get_connection_manager()` to a file the gate scans, run it again (expect FAIL naming that file), revert the probe, run once more (expect PASS). Confirm `git status` is clean for the probed file before committing.

## REQUIRED — I2: the spec asserts something false about a fail-closed authentication path

`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-sma-473-redis-retry-budget-design.md:171-173` (D6) says: *"This changes **only how fast** the JWKS path fails; the D15 fail-closed posture is untouched and stays correct."* That is false.

Mechanism: when the shared connection future is being re-established, the first command awaits the whole `backon` schedule. **Pre-fix that schedule ran up to ~9.5 s, so a Redis blip or failover shorter than it was absorbed and the command SUCCEEDED** (slowly). Post-fix the absorption window is one 100–200 ms retry.

- On the authz path that is a cache bypass — fail-open, harmless, and the spec's residual list already records it.
- On `authn.jwks_cache.backend = "redis"` the identical event is a **503 on every token-authenticated request**, because `RedisJwksCache::get`'s error is `?`-propagated out of `JwksProvider::cache_state` (`rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/oidc/jwks.rs:249`) before any refetch is attempted.

Concrete scenario to capture: a routine 2 s Redis primary failover. Before, authentication was unaffected. After, every OIDC-bearer request 503s for those 2 s, and **neither** alert fires (both are `for: 10m`).

**Fix (documentation + conscious acceptance, no code change):**
1. Correct D6 in the spec — it changes how fast *and* how often the JWKS path fails. State the trade explicitly and accept it.
2. Widen the spec's residual-risk entry (currently written only for the fail-open half) to cover the fail-closed half.
3. Add a sentence to the RUNBOOK's JWKS paragraph (`docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:796`) so an operator can predict this: short Redis blips that used to be invisible now surface as brief authentication 503s, below both alerts' `for:` windows.
4. Note in the spec that D8's single shared `connection_manager_config()` currently forbids giving the fail-closed path a larger connect budget than the fail-open one, and that this is an accepted consequence rather than an oversight.

## Also fix — all one-clause corrections

**M3 — `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:541-545`: the "ten straight minutes" arithmetic is wrong by 2×.** `rate(...[5m])` stays `> 0` for a full 5 m after the *last* bypass sample, so `for: 10m` is satisfied by a bypass window of only ~5 minutes. Both "bypassed entirely for ten straight minutes" and "Ten minutes of it means the Redis backend is unhealthy" overstate. The `for: 10m` choice stays — only the explanation changes. This is the first thing a paged operator reads.

**M4 — `ops/observability/prometheus/rules/iam.rules.yml:79`, two errors in one comment.**
(a) It says `~20-30s`; every other file settled on **19–28 s**. This is the last inconsistent number in the branch.
(b) It claims the outage "tripped `IamHighErrorRate`". It could not have: `serve_http` (`rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/http/mod.rs:733-735`) applies `TimeoutLayer` *outside* `app_routes`, which carries `http_metrics_layer` inside it — a timed-out request short-circuits at 408 before the metrics layer records anything, so `iam_http_requests_total` never counts it; and 408 is `status_class="4xx"` while the rule filters `5xx`. The **gRPC** half (`IamGrpcHighErrorRate`) does hold. Correct the claim to the gRPC signal and client-side timeouts. (This strengthens the case for the new alert — the old HTTP signal was weaker than we credited it.) Check whether the same framing at RUNBOOK `:783-786` needs the same correction.

**M5 — two different per-decision bounds.** RUNBOOK `:548`, `:707`, `:1125` say ~0.2–0.8 s per authz decision; `cedar_authorizer.rs:45` says ~0.2–0.6 s. The 0.8 s upper end actually comes from the *revoke* row (a mutation), not any decision row. Adopt one formulation everywhere: *0.2–0.6 s per decision; 0.3–0.8 s per authz-mutating request; up to ~1.2 s for a gated cross-principal decision.*

**M7 — the spec no longer describes the shipped gate.** `…design.md:358-359` and `:468` still say the gate asserts `new_lazy_with_config` appears only in `redis_conn.rs`. The shipped gate deliberately exempts it (two `#[cfg(test)]` sites legitimately call it with `connection_manager_config()`). Update both to describe what actually ships, including the I1 term you are adding.

**M8 — `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:725-726`** says the timeouts are "both applied to every attempt by `new_lazy_with_config`". Production now uses `new_with_config`, and both constructors apply them identically. Fix the attribution.

**M9 — the alert's Confirm steps omit the capacity risk the fix creates.** `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md:577-596`. Removing the retry latency also removes the accidental ~50× throttle it imposed, so during an outage the *uncached* decision rate hitting Postgres is now full traffic rather than a trickle. Not silent (pool saturation → 5xx → `IamHighErrorRate`), so not a correctness problem — but "check Postgres connection-pool headroom" belongs in **Confirm**, because it is the failure mode this change newly enables.

**M10 — `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/http/mod.rs:626-628`** says "when it can't reuse an already-open `redis_conn`", referring to the local binding at `:291`. There is now also a module `crate::adapters::redis_conn`. Add a word of disambiguation.

**M11 — close an open spec question.** The spec (`…design.md:428-430`) records as **Unverified** whether `connection_timeout` wraps DNS resolution. **It does:** `redis-1.3.0/src/client.rs:505-510` wraps the whole `get_multiplexed_async_connection_inner` — address resolution included — in `rt.timeout(connection_timeout, …)`. So the ~2.1 s blackhole figure holds for a hung resolver too. Restate it as verified, with that citation.

**D10 orchestrator caveat.** The spec's boot-tolerance reasoning leans on "container restart backoff (10 s → 20 s → 40 s)", which is Kubernetes `CrashLoopBackOff` specifically. This repo ships no deployment manifest for IAM, so nothing guarantees it — under a supervisor with a fixed short restart delay, IAM now crash-loops far faster than before during a Redis outage. RUNBOOK `:780-781` already says "Depend on the orchestrator's restart policy"; make it say to **verify your orchestrator actually has backoff**.

**Folded deferred minors (same files, no extra cost):**
- `moon.yml:165-167` — the `expected`-control comment says a rename "would make BOTH greps empty". Wrong: a rename trips the `expected` control and exits 2. Correct it.
- RUNBOOK `:769` — "unlike the table above" implies the whole table is measured; only the 28.4 s cell is. Suggested: "unlike the stopped/refused shape above, which has been exercised end-to-end".
- RUNBOOK `:548-549` — pairs the new cross-principal "after" number with the old self-query "before" (19–28 s); the cross-principal before is ~38–57 s. Fix while doing M5, which touches the same clause.

**Do NOT change:** "~50× sooner", "~10× the table", prose line widths, or the alias-evasion gap in the gate (deliberate non-goals).

```
cargo fmt --check
promtool check rules ops/observability/prometheus/rules/*.rules.yml

```

1	# SMA-473 — Bound the Redis client retry budget
2	
3	**Status:** design (revised after adversarial review)
4	**Date:** 2026-08-02
5	**Issue:** [SMA-473](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-473/iam-bound-the-redis-client-retry-budget-an-outage-costs-20-30s-per)
6	**Project:** Paigasus IAM
7	**Follows:** [SMA-470](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-470/iam-cover-revocation-during-redis-outage-and-decide-whether-to-offer-a) (found while implementing it)
8	
9	## 1. Problem
10	
11	`paigasus-iam` opens every Redis connection with a bare `ConnectionManager::new(client)`,
12	i.e. a stock `ConnectionManagerConfig::default()`. Against a **down** backend that default
13	costs ~6.3–12.6 s per failed command, and a single authz decision makes several such reads.
14	Measured on a real stopped-Redis container (the SMA-470 acceptance test):
15	
16	| request | measured | cycles |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `POST /v1/authz/is-authorized` | **19–28 s** | 2–3 |
19	| `DELETE /v1/authz/role-grants/{id}` (revoke) | **28.4 s** | 3–4 |
20	
21	The authz stack is deliberately fail-open on a Redis outage (SMA-470 D1: Redis is a pure
22	accelerator, so denying during its outage would convert a latency degradation into a total
23	authorization outage). That reasoning holds only if the degradation is *small*. At 20–30 s
24	per decision nearly every caller times out anyway, so operationally the outage is much
25	closer to an authz outage than to a degradation. **Bounding the retry budget restores D1's
26	premise; it does not weaken it.**
27	
28	### 1.1 The mechanism, precisely
29	
30	Read from `redis-1.3.0/src/aio/connection_manager.rs` and `backon-1.6.0`:
31	
32	- `ConnectionManager` holds an `ArcSwap`'d **shared connection future**. Every command
33	  (`send_packed_command`, `connection_manager.rs:678`) loads and awaits it.
34	- When Redis is down that future is a `new_connection` running the full `backon` retry
35	  schedule before resolving to `Err`.
36	- The resulting I/O error triggers `Self::reconnect`, which CAS-swaps in a **fresh** future
37	  and spawns it **detached** (`connection_manager.rs:649`); the failing command returns
38	  immediately without awaiting it. The next command therefore awaits a brand-new cycle.
39	
40	**The retry budget covers establishing a connection, never a command.**
41	`send_packed_command` does `connection_result?.send_packed_command(cmd).await` and then
42	`reconnect_if_dropped!`, which triggers a background reconnect and **returns the `Err` to
43	the caller** (`connection_manager.rs:390-398`). No command is ever retried. This matters
44	because it is the only thing `number_of_retries` buys (see D2).
45	
46	**"One cycle per failed command" is an upper bound for a specific code shape**, not an
47	identity. It holds for a single in-flight request issuing reads back-to-back with no
48	intervening work — which is exactly what `is_authorized` does. It does **not** hold for
49	*concurrent* commands: they all await the same `Shared` future and only the CAS winner
50	spawns the replacement, so N concurrent reads cost one cycle, not N.
51	
52	*Independently measured:* the existing Docker-free unit test
53	`api_keys::cache::tests::redis_cache_fails_open_when_the_backend_is_unreachable` issues
54	`get` + `put` + `evict` against a closed port and takes **28.403 s** — 9.47 s per cycle,
55	squarely in the predicted 6.3–12.6 s band with an expected ~9.5 s. The model is confirmed by
56	something other than the SMA-470 measurement it was derived from.
57	
58	**The cost is the retry schedule, not the per-attempt timeouts.** redis-rs 1.3.0 already
59	defaults `connection_timeout` to 1 s and `response_timeout` to 500 ms
60	(`DEFAULT_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT` / `DEFAULT_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT`). What is unbounded *in practice*
61	is `number_of_retries = 6`, `min_delay = 100 ms`, `exponent_base = 2.0` — a
62	`100+200+400+800+1600+3200 ms` schedule, ~6.3 s per cycle as a floor.
63	
64	**Two `backon` details determine which knob actually moves the number:**
65	
66	1. **Jitter *adds*.** `ExponentialBackoff::next` computes
67	   `tmp_cur = tmp_cur + tmp_cur.mul_f32(rng.f32())` (`exponential.rs:234`), so an actual
68	   sleep is `delay × [1.0, 2.0]` — a cycle is 6.3–12.6 s, expected ~9.5 s. (redis-rs
69	   documents `min(max_delay, rand(0 .. min_delay * base^try))`, which describes neither the
70	   addition nor point 2.)
71	2. **`max_delay` caps the *pre-jitter base* delay, and never applies to the first step.**
72	   When `current_delay` is `None` the code returns `self.min_delay` directly
73	   (`exponential.rs:210-213`), bypassing the clamp. So at `number_of_retries = 1` there is
74	   exactly **one** sleep, it is `min_delay × [1,2]`, and `max_delay` is **inert**.
75	
76	Note the schedule is not literally unbounded even today: redis's `ConnectionManagerConfig`
77	leaves `max_delay` at `None`, so `backon`'s own `ExponentialBuilder::new()` default of
78	`Some(60 s)` applies (`exponential.rs:61`) — inert here, because a 6-step schedule peaks at
79	3.2 s. Consequence: **`number_of_retries` is the only lever that moves the measured number.**
80	
81	### 1.2 What reading the code found beyond the issue
82	
83	The issue names one call site. There are **two** production sites, and the unnamed one is
84	worse.
85	
86	`RedisJwksCache::connect` (`adapters/oidc/redis_cache.rs:42`, wired at
87	`adapters/http/mod.rs:568`) uses the same bare `ConnectionManager::new(client)`. Unlike the
88	authz caches it does **not** fail open: `RedisJwksCache::get` maps any Redis error to
89	`AuthnError::Unavailable` (spec §4.3/D15 — key material, so fail-closed is correct), and
90	`JwksProvider::key_for` reads the cache on **every** token validation
91	(`adapters/oidc/jwks.rs:207,249`).
92	
93	So under `authn.jwks_cache.backend = "redis"`, a Redis outage makes every authenticated
94	request burn a full ~6–12 s reconnect cycle **and then 503**. That is a hard authentication
95	outage with ~10 s of latency bolted on. The RUNBOOK's availability section documents only
96	the authz cost and never mentions it.
97	
98	A third path shares the same handle and is also undocumented: `RedisApiKeyCache`
99	(`adapters/http/mod.rs:468-490`) is read on **every** API-key-authenticated request. A miss
100	costs a `get` **and** a `put` (2 cycles); `RevokeApiKey` / `ArchiveServiceAccount` add an
101	`evict`. The RUNBOOK itself calls the gateway's `IntrospectApiKey`/`IsAuthorized` pair "the
102	hottest gRPC path in normal operation" (`RUNBOOK-observability.md:520-522`).
103	
104	### 1.3 Evidence
105	
106	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/http/mod.rs:628` — `connect_redis`, bare
107	  `ConnectionManager::new`.
108	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/oidc/redis_cache.rs:42` —
109	  `RedisJwksCache::connect`, same.
110	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/oidc/jwks.rs:207,249` — per-token cache read;

112	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/application/authorize.rs:76-79` — `decide_gated` runs
113	  a full second `is_authorized` for a non-self query.
114	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/src/adapters/authz/policy_snapshot.rs:209-214` —

116	- `rs/crates/services/paigasus-iam/tests/authz_acceptance.rs:705` — the measurement and the

118	- `ops/observability/prometheus/rules/iam.rules.yml` — eight alerts, **none** on

120	- `docs/ops/RUNBOOK-observability.md` §"Authz availability posture" — documents the current
121	  cost and names SMA-473 as the unshipped mitigation.
122	
123	## 2. Decisions
124	
125	**D1 — Cap the retry count only; leave every timeout at the redis-rs default.**
126	`number_of_retries` 6 → **1**. `min_delay` (100 ms), `exponent_base`, `connection_timeout`
127	(1 s) and `response_timeout` (500 ms) are all left alone. The two timeouts are what the
128	issue explicitly warns off, and they are already bounded.
129
